_comment: Laparoscopic access, survey and closure. Shared by every laparoscopic procedure.

step.lap.access.title: Establishing pneumoperitoneum
step.lap.access.why: Access is where laparoscopy injures people. Vascular and bowel injuries at entry are rare, are usually caused blind, and are frequently recognised late.
how: Prefer an open (Hasson) cut-down in a previously operated abdomen, in the very thin and in the very obese.
Empty the stomach and the bladder before entry.
If using a Veress needle, insert at a site away from scars, confirm position by low opening pressure and free flow rather than by feel alone.
Insufflate to the working pressure gradually and watch the airway pressure and the capnograph as you go.
structuresAtRisk: Aorta and inferior vena cava at the umbilicus in a thin patient
Small bowel adherent to a previous scar
Inferior epigastric vessels at the lateral port sites
pitfalls: A high opening pressure interpreted as 'the abdomen is stiff' rather than as a misplaced needle.

step.lap.ports.title: Port placement
step.lap.ports.why: Ports placed for the anatomy you have, rather than for the textbook, are the difference between a comfortable operation and a fight.
how: Place the camera port first, inspect beneath the intended sites, then place every subsequent port under direct vision.
Transilluminate the abdominal wall to avoid the inferior epigastric vessels.
Triangulate: keep working ports about a hand's breadth apart and aimed at the target.
structuresAtRisk: Bowel adherent to the anterior abdominal wall
pitfalls: Ports placed too close together, so the instruments fight each other.
A port placed without looking at what lies under it.

step.lap.survey.title: Diagnostic laparoscopy and survey
step.lap.survey.why: The first look answers a question the imaging could not, and it is the only chance to find the second diagnosis before attention narrows to the first.
how: Before touching the target, look at the liver, gallbladder, stomach, small bowel, colon, pelvis and both paracolic gutters.
Note the character and volume of any free fluid, and aspirate it for culture where relevant.
In a woman of childbearing age, inspect the tubes and ovaries explicitly.
pitfalls: Going straight to the target and missing a second pathology.
Recording 'diagnostic laparoscopy normal' without saying what was actually seen.

step.lap.specimen-retrieval.title: Specimen retrieval
step.lap.specimen-retrieval.why: Bringing an infected or neoplastic specimen through the abdominal wall unprotected causes port-site infection and, in malignancy, port-site recurrence.
how: Use a retrieval bag for any infected, perforated or potentially malignant specimen.
Extract through the largest port, extending the fascial incision rather than tearing the bag.
Inspect the bag afterwards to confirm the specimen is intact and nothing has been left behind.
pitfalls: A bag torn during extraction, spilling contents into the wound.
Enlarging the skin but not the fascia.

step.lap.closure.title: Desufflation and port-site closure
step.lap.closure.why: A port-site hernia through an unclosed 10 mm fascial defect can strangulate, and it presents days later to someone who was not in theatre.
how: Inspect the operative field again at low insufflation pressure: bleeding tamponaded by pneumoperitoneum appears as the pressure falls.
Remove ports under vision and check each site from inside for bleeding.
Close the fascia at every port of 10 mm or more, and at any site where the fascia has been stretched.
Desufflate fully to reduce shoulder-tip pain.
structuresAtRisk: Bowel caught in a fascial suture placed blind
pitfalls: Removing all ports at once with the camera already out.
Closing skin over an unclosed 10 mm fascial defect.
